target: आदाब अर्ज़ है, मिज़ाज शरीफ़?
english: My respects to you; how is your health?
tip: आदाब अर्ज़ है (aadaab arz hai) is literally 'respects are presented' – a courtly Urdu-style greeting you'll hear among Urdu speakers and in formal, old-school settings.

target: देखो, बारिश होने वाली है।
english: Look, it's about to rain.
tip: होने वाली है (hone vaali hai) = 'is about to happen'. Verb + वाला (vaala) marks something on the verge – the same वाला (vaala) that usually means 'the one who'.

target: ताला लगाकर चाबी सुरक्षित रखो।
english: Lock it and keep the key safe.
tip: -कर (-kar) on a verb means 'having done it': ताला लगाकर (taala lagaakar = having locked). Hindi links actions this way where English says 'and then'.

target: शायद वो कल तक आ जाए।
english: Perhaps he'll come by tomorrow.
tip: Position words follow their noun: कल तक (kal tak) is literally 'tomorrow by' = 'by tomorrow'. Flip the English order every time.

target: उसे तो पहले से ही पता था।
english: He already knew it.
tip: तो (to) after a word isn't 'then' – it stresses that word: उसे तो (use to = as for him) – he, of all people, already knew.

target: कम से कम एक बार तो कोशिश करो।
english: At least try once.
tip: कम से कम (kam se kam) is literally 'less than less' – Hindi's way of saying 'at least'. The mirror phrase ज़्यादा से ज़्यादा (zyaada se zyaada) = at most.

target: काश मुझे पहले पता होता!
english: I wish I had known earlier!
tip: काश (kaash) = 'if only'. काश मुझे पहले पता होता (kaash mujhe pehle pataa hotaa = if only I'd known earlier) – the bare -ता (-taa) form marks a wish that didn't come true.

target: यह काम मुझसे ही होगा।
english: Only I can do this work.
tip: ही (hi) narrows to 'only/exactly': मुझसे ही होगा (mujhse hi hoga) = it will get done only by me. It's sharper than English 'just'.

target: अच्छा, तो डॉक्टर ने क्या कहा?
english: Okay, so what did the doctor say?
tip: अच्छा (achchhaa) literally means 'good', but opening a sentence it works as 'okay / oh / I see' – here it's just moving the conversation along, not praising anything.

target: राजेश ने आज नई कमीज़ ख़रीदी।
english: Rajesh bought a new shirt today.
tip: After ने (ne), the verb agrees with the object. मैंने रोटी खाई (mainne roti khaai = I ate bread, f sg). मैंने रोटियाँ खाईं (mainne rotiyaan khaaeen = plural). Subject doesn't matter.

target: अरे वाह, तुमने तो कमाल कर दिया!
english: Wow, you did an amazing job!
tip: तो (to) adds attitude – contrast or emphasis, like 'well' or 'really': तुमने तो कमाल कर दिया (tumne to kamaal kar diya) = you really pulled it off.

target: अरे, फ़ोन की बैटरी ख़त्म हो गई।
english: Oh no, the phone's battery died.
tip: Hindi adds 'went' to say something is fully over: ख़त्म हो गई (khatm ho gayi = became finished, went). That little गई (gayi = went) marks the change as complete.

target: तुम भी चलो, अकेले मज़ा नहीं आता।
english: You also come, it's no fun alone.
tip: भी (bhi = also/too) sits right after the word it stresses: तुम भी चलो (tum bhi chalo) = you come too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.

target: ठीक है, मैं तुम्हें बाद में फ़ोन करता हूँ।
english: Okay, I'll call you later.
tip: करता हूँ (kartaa hoon) is present tense – literally 'I call' – but it means 'I'll call'. Hindi uses the plain present for things you're about to do.

target: हे भगवान, चाबी कहीं मिल नहीं रही।
english: Oh God, I can't find the keys anywhere.
tip: You don't find things in Hindi – they 'meet' you: चाबी कहीं मिल नहीं रही (chaabi kaheen mil nahin rahi = the key isn't turning up anywhere). The same verb मिल (mil) is used for meeting people.

target: चलिए सरला जी, अंदर चलते हैं।
english: Come Sarla ji, let's go inside.
tip: जी (ji) after a name adds respect: सरला जी (Sarla ji) works like a built-in 'ma'am'. It also makes yes and no politer: हाँ जी (haan ji), ना जी (naa ji).

target: बस, अब और नहीं सहा जाता।
english: Enough, I can't take it anymore.
tip: बस (bas) here isn't the vehicle – it means 'enough, no more'. The same word also means 'just/only', so context decides which बस (bas) you're hearing.

target: विकास कल कोलकाता गया।
english: Vikas went to Kolkata yesterday.
tip: No ने (ne) on the doer here: विकास (Vikas) just गया (gayaa = went). Going acts on nothing, so the doer stays plain. Ne appears only when the action lands on a thing.

target: डाकिए ने सुबह-सुबह चिट्ठी दी।
english: The postman delivered the letter early in the morning.
tip: Doubling often intensifies: सुबह-सुबह (subah-subah = morning-morning) means very early, at the crack of dawn. Repeating a word is a normal grammar move in Hindi.

target: श्याम ने नई नौकरी शुरू की।
english: Shyam started a new job.
tip: Past-tense doers take ने (ne): श्याम ने नई नौकरी शुरू की (Shyam ne naee naukree shuru kee = Shyam started a new job). Ne appears only when the action lands on something.

target: विनोद ने पुरानी किताबें बेच दीं।
english: Vinod sold the old books.
tip: बेच दीं (bech deen = sold off) ends in a nasal sound because किताबें (kitaaben = books) is feminine plural – the verb tracks the books, and the tiny dot is its only plural clue.

target: भाई साहब, आपसे मिलकर बड़ी ख़ुशी हुई।
english: Brother, it's been a pleasure meeting you.
tip: Joy happens TO you in Hindi: ख़ुशी हुई (khushee huee = happiness occurred). You aren't glad – gladness arrived. The set phrase for being pleased to meet someone.

target: हवाई अड्डे पर सामान की जाँच हुई।
english: The baggage was inspected at the airport.
tip: No 'was inspected' – Hindi says the check happened: जाँच हुई (jaanch huee = inspection happened). When the doer doesn't matter, things simply occur.

target: अंजलि ने दिल्ली का टिकट ऑनलाइन बुक किया।
english: Anjali booked the ticket to Delhi online.
tip: English words become verbs with किया (kiyaa = did): बुक किया (buk kiyaa) = booked. The loanword stays a noun; करना (karnaa = to do) does the verb work – recharge kiyaa, cancel kiyaa.

target: बच्चों ने बिना किसी मदद के घर साफ़ किया।
english: The children cleaned the house without any help.
tip: 'Without' wraps its noun from both sides: बिना किसी मदद के (binaa kisee madad ke) – binaa before, ke after. English says 'without' once; Hindi closes the bracket.

target: ड्राइवर ने गाड़ी तेज़ चलाई।
english: The driver drove the car fast.
tip: Hindi has no verb 'drive' – you make the vehicle go: गाड़ी तेज़ चलाई (gaadee tez chalaaee = drove the car fast). चलाना (chalaanaa = make move) also runs shops and machines.

target: सुनीता जी, आपसे मिलकर बहुत खुशी हुई।
english: Sunita, I'm really happy to have met you.
tip: जी (jee) after a name adds warmth and respect: सुनीता जी (Suneetaa jee). It attaches to any name – and even to yes and no: haan jee, nahin jee.

target: डॉक्टर ने मुझे तीन दिन आराम करने को कहा।
english: The doctor told me to rest for three days.
tip: 'Told me to rest' = आराम करने को कहा (aaraam karne ko kahaa) – literally 'said for doing rest'. Orders and requests use karne ko, not a plain to-verb.

target: बच्चों ने पूरा खाना खा लिया।
english: The children ate all the food.
tip: खा लिया (khaa liyaa) adds लेना (lenaa = take) to eating – it signals the food is finished, gone. Plain खाया (khaayaa) just says eating happened, with no sense of completion.

target: तीसरे दिन हम शिमला पहुँच गए।
english: On the third day, we reached Shimla.
tip: 'Reached Shimla' sounds like it acts on Shimla, but पहुँच गए (pahunch gaye) takes no ने (ne) – arriving counts as pure motion in Hindi, like going and coming.
